summary: Abraham has further children with Keturah, gives Isaac the chief inheritance while sending other sons east with gifts, and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael. Ishmael’s twelve sons and death are recorded; the account then turns to Isaac and Rebekah, whose struggling twins receive an oracle before birth, and ends when hungry Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a meal.
whyItMatters: Several branches of Abraham’s family remain visible before the narrative narrows to the next contested household. The oracle and birthright exchange introduce the sibling struggle that shapes the following chapters.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The burial cave near Mamre, Ishmael’s wider settlements, and Isaac and Rebekah’s household.
context.literaryForm: Interlocking family genealogies and death notices followed by twin-birth and birthright narratives.

before.text: Rebekah has traveled from Abraham’s relatives and become Isaac’s wife after Sarah’s death. The next chapter records other family lines before focusing on their sons.

here.text: Follow the shifts among Keturah’s descendants, Abraham’s burial, Ishmael’s twelve princes, and Isaac’s twins; the birthright scene closes this chapter.

after.text: A famine brings Isaac to Gerar, where God renews the family promise and Isaac repeats a dangerous wife-sister claim.

outline.heading: Keturah’s children and distribution
outline.note: Abraham’s other descendants are named, while Isaac receives the main estate and others gifts.

outline.heading: Abraham’s death and burial
outline.note: Isaac and Ishmael bury him with Sarah; Isaac receives blessing.

outline.heading: Ishmael’s sons, settlements, and death
outline.note: Twelve princes and their territories complete this line.

outline.heading: Isaac and Rebekah’s twins
outline.note: After prayer for conception, Rebekah receives an oracle and bears Esau and Jacob.

outline.heading: Unequal affection and birthright sale
outline.note: The brothers differ in work and parental favor; Esau sells his birthright for food.

keyVerses.text: Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is near Mamre,
keyVerses.why: Isaac and Ishmael are both present to bury their father.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh said to her, “Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples will be separated from your body. The one people will be stronger than the other people. The elder will serve the younger.”
keyVerses.why: The oracle names two peoples and reverses the expected senior-junior relation.

keyVerses.text: Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way. So Esau despised his birthright.
keyVerses.why: The closing judgment says Esau despised the birthright after the meal and oath.

questions.question: What happens to Abraham’s children besides Isaac?
questions.answer: The chapter names sons with Keturah and says Abraham gives gifts to the sons of his concubines and sends them east. Isaac receives all that Abraham has as the chief inheritance, so the distribution is unequal and explicit.

questions.question: Does the burial scene erase the earlier expulsion of Ishmael?
questions.answer: No. Isaac and Ishmael appear together to bury Abraham, but the chapter does not narrate a reconciliation conversation or undo Hagar and Ishmael’s earlier displacement. Both the joint burial and the earlier harm remain in the book.

questions.question: What are the “twelve princes” in Ishmael’s line?
questions.answer: They are the leaders associated with Ishmael’s twelve named sons, villages, encampments, and nations. The list fulfills the promise of many descendants without identifying every later population with certainty.

questions.question: How does Rebekah become pregnant after infertility?
questions.answer: The text says Isaac entreats Yahweh for his wife because she is barren, and Yahweh responds so she conceives. When the twins struggle, Rebekah herself goes to inquire and receives a speech about their futures.

questions.question: Does the oracle tell either brother to deceive or harm the other?
questions.answer: It says two peoples are in Rebekah’s womb and the elder will serve the younger. It does not instruct Jacob to bargain for a birthright or authorize later manipulation; those actions have to be assessed where the narrative reports them.

questions.question: What is a “birthright” in the stew exchange?
questions.answer: It is the elder brother’s status and expected inheritance claim that Jacob asks Esau to sell. The chapter does not list every legal entitlement, but it treats the oath and transfer as weightier than an ordinary bowl of food.

questions.question: Does hunger make Esau’s sale a fair bargain?
questions.answer: Esau says he is famished and asks for food, while Jacob makes the sale and oath a condition before feeding him. The narrator ends by saying Esau despised his birthright, yet the account also lets readers see Jacob’s use of a hungry moment.

questions.question: Why name both parents’ preferences?
questions.answer: Isaac loves Esau for his venison, while Rebekah loves Jacob. The brief notice places the brothers’ later exchange within a divided household rather than presenting their rivalry as isolated from family relationships.

glossary.def: The elder son’s claim that Jacob demands Esau sell for a meal.
The woman named as Abraham’s later wife and mother of several listed sons.
The location where Isaac lives after Abraham’s death, previously named in Hagar’s story.
